title: Japan's Newspaper Subscription Rate Falls Below 50%
paragraphs: Japan has long been known as a country of newspaper readers. But for the first time, fewer than half of people in Japan now subscribe to a newspaper, according to a new survey.

The survey was carried out by the Japan Press Research Institute in the summer of 2026. It sent questions to 5,000 randomly selected people, and 2,676 of them answered. The results were reported in October.

The survey found that 49.8% of people have a monthly newspaper subscription. This is 0.3 percentage points lower than the year before. It is also a huge drop from 2008, when the survey began. At that time, the rate was 88.6%.

There was a big difference between age groups. More than 70% of people aged 70 or older subscribe to a newspaper. But among people in their 20s and 40s, the rate was only around 30%, and among people in their 30s, it was about 20%.

The survey also asked people who do not subscribe why they do not. The most common reason, given by 73.7%, was that television, the internet and other sources give them enough news. Some people also mentioned the cost and their reading habits.
In addition, the share of people who read news in a newspaper at least once a week also fell below half for the first time, to 49.7%.

However, many people in Japan still trust newspapers. The survey asked people to rate how much they trust different types of media on a scale of 100. Newspapers scored 64.6 points, coming in second place after the public broadcaster NHK's television news, which scored 66.1. The internet scored less than 50 points.
The results show that although fewer people are paying for newspapers, many still see them as a reliable source of information.
